input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-420: Principles of Data Mining. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. Source excerpts:

[postgresql-documentation]
Data systems organize records with declared types, tables, rows, columns, keys, and constraints. Queries select, join, aggregate, order, and transform data. Indexes provide additional access paths for selected workloads. Transactions group operations and isolation controls how concurrent operations observe one another. Query planning and physical storage affect performance without changing logical query meaning. Analytical work should preserve provenance from captured data through cleaning, transformation, grouping, modeling, visualization, and reporting. Data quality analysis makes missingness, duplicates, inconsistent representation, integrity constraints, sampling, and update behavior explicit.

Topics include knowledge discovery process; data exploration and cleaning; and data mining algorithms. The emphasis is on how to use data mining to describe datasets rather than making predictions. Data mining projects and a term paper are required. Prerequisites: CSCI-320 and (STAT-145 or MATH-251 or STAT-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students may not take this course if they have received credit for CSCI-420H or CSCI-620. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Data-analysis workflows separate data preparation, exploratory analysis, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine transformations and estimators so the same operations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined splits. Grouping, dimensionality reduction, classification, regression, and clustering answer different questions and require appropriate assumptions and metrics. Evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors, while distribution shift, missing data, overfitting, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions.

beats.claim: Real-world datasets are often large and can be stored in either main memory or a database.
beats.example: Student teams will load a 100,000-row customer transaction dataset into a relational database for initial exploration.
beats.title: Course Foundations and Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a split-screen graphic showing a database schema on the left and an in-memory DataFrame on the right, with arrows indicating data flow between storage types.

beats.claim: The knowledge discovery process involves using data mining to describe datasets rather than making predictions.
beats.example: Instructors will demonstrate how clustering customer purchase patterns reveals market segments without forecasting future sales.
beats.title: Knowledge Discovery Process
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart labeled 'Knowledge Discovery Process' with nodes for data collection, cleaning, analysis, and description, explicitly excluding a 'prediction' node.

beats.claim: Data quality analysis makes missingness, duplicates, inconsistent representation, integrity constraints, and sampling explicit.
beats.example: Students will run a missingness report on a survey dataset, flagging 15% null values in the 'income' column and removing 3% duplicate records.
beats.title: Data Exploration and Cleaning
beats.visualDirection: Render a heatmap of missing values across columns, with a callout box highlighting the 'income' column and a duplicate count badge.

beats.claim: Data-analysis workflows separate data preparation, exploratory analysis, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation.
beats.example: A pipeline will be built where raw data undergoes imputation and normalization before entering the exploratory analysis phase.
beats.title: Data Preparation Workflows
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a horizontal pipeline diagram with seven distinct stages, each labeled with a workflow phase and connected by directional arrows.

beats.claim: Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets.
beats.example: Students will compare a decision tree trained on labeled customer churn data against a k-means clustering run on the same unlabeled features.
beats.title: Supervised and Unsupervised Methods
beats.visualDirection: Display two side-by-side scatter plots: one with labeled points and a decision boundary, the other with unlabeled points and cluster centroids.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage.
beats.example: Instructors will demonstrate scaling a feature using only the training set statistics, then applying the same transformation to the validation set.
beats.title: Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Show a before-and-after comparison of a feature distribution, with a red 'leakage' warning icon over a graph where validation statistics were incorrectly used for scaling.

beats.claim: Pipelines combine transformations and estimators so the same operations are applied consistently.
beats.example: A single pipeline object will chain standardization, imputation, and clustering, ensuring identical operations run on every data split.
beats.title: Pipelines and Consistency
beats.visualDirection: Render a stacked block diagram where each layer represents a transformation or estimator, with a 'consistent application' label spanning the entire stack.

beats.claim: Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined splits to assess model stability.
beats.example: Students will execute a 5-fold cross-validation routine, rotating the validation set through each dataset partition and recording accuracy scores.
beats.title: Cross-Validation and Sampling
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a circular diagram with five segments, each labeled with a fold number, and arrows showing data rotation between training and validation phases.

beats.claim: Grouping, dimensionality reduction, classification, regression, and clustering answer different questions and require appropriate assumptions and metrics.
beats.example: Instructors will match a regression model to predicting continuous revenue and a clustering algorithm to segment user behavior, explaining the distinct evaluation metrics for each.
beats.title: Algorithm Selection and Evaluation
beats.visualDirection: Display a decision tree flowchart where each branch leads to an algorithm type, with corresponding metric badges (e.g., RMSE, silhouette score) attached to each leaf.

beats.claim: Distribution shift, missing data, overfitting, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions.
beats.example: Students will complete a checklist verifying data provenance, checking for distribution drift between train and test sets, and documenting sampling methodology.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a clean checklist graphic with five checkboxes, each paired with a brief validation step, and a final 'valid conclusions' stamp icon.

learningObjectives: Define the knowledge discovery process and distinguish descriptive data mining from predictive modeling.
Explain data exploration and cleaning techniques, including handling missingness, duplicates, and inconsistent representation.
Apply data mining algorithms for grouping, dimensionality reduction, classification, regression, and clustering to describe datasets.

Next, compare the choices involved in Data Preparation Workflows and make the decision criteria explicit. Now define Knowledge Discovery Process precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. The emphasis is on how to use data mining to describe datasets rather than making predictions.
